problem: VLA models build action heads directly on pretrained vision-language backbones, so action-loss gradients flow broadly into the inherited multimodal pathway. This can destabilize language-side processing and object grounding, which shows up as unstable instruction generation and weak grounding under real-scene visual shift.
motivation: Action supervision does more than train a downstream decoder; it reshapes inherited representations. That reshaping is needed for action-compatible features but can be disruptive when applied too directly. Zero-shot sim-to-real closed-loop navigation exposes the resulting instability, because instruction errors compound into trajectory divergence and task failure.
key_idea: Insert a query-based action-facing interface (Action QFormer) between the VLM backbone and the policy head, so that instruction-conditioned learnable queries select visual evidence and give action-loss gradients an intermediate adaptation route before they reach the inherited pathway.
insight: Gradient-blocking diagnostics show the left-right distinction forms only when action loss reaches the upstream pathway (full update); Action QFormer sharpens it (action-repr cosine 0.520 vs 0.931 for direct fusion) while reducing rewriting magnitude and spread and keeping instruction-to-visual attention more stable. With instructions given, the baseline recovers much of its success, so most of the closed-loop gap comes from instruction instability. The visual-source and query-only ablations show that both the pre-fusion visual embedding and explicit instruction context matter.
method: Direct-fusion baseline: self-attention over concatenated image-side and instruction-side hidden states from Qwen2.5-VL, pooled into an action-facing latent that goes to a diffusion policy head.

Action QFormer: 16 learnable queries and 4 layers. Each layer runs self-attention over [queries; instruction tokens], keeps the query outputs, then cross-attends to image tokens. Pooled queries are combined with the instruction representation into z_t. The default visual source is the vision-encoder embedding, not the post-LLM image latent.

Policy head and objective: a conditional diffusion head predicts an 8-step local-frame trajectory (x, y, yaw_dx, yaw_dy). The loss is (1-r)L_action + r L_lang, with r cosine-scheduled from high to low, so language supervision comes first and action supervision is ramped up.
Supervision data: single-frame Habitat ObjectNav data, with GPT-generated one-sentence navigation instructions (object and non-object templates) conditioned on the image and the future trajectory.

Closed-loop inference: the backbone first generates an intermediate instruction, boundary markers extract image and instruction spans, the interface builds z_t, and the diffusion head samples a trajectory that is executed.

Gradient-routing diagnostics: stop-gradient settings (action-update-blocked, vision-encoder-frozen, language-backbone-blocked, full update) are compared against the blocked reference using Fisher score and cosine for the left-right distinction, token drift energy, effective rank, and attention reference-region mass and center shift.

setting.backbone: Qwen2.5-VL (fine-tuned) + Action QFormer / latent-fuser interface + diffusion policy head
setting.training_data: Habitat ObjectNav training dataset, single current frame, with GPT-generated instructions and 8-step local-frame trajectories; 6000 steps, no other navigation data
setting.observation: single current-frame monocular RGB plus task text
setting.action_space: predicted 8-step local-frame trajectory (x, y, yaw direction vector) from a diffusion policy, executed by a controller
setting.simulator: Habitat (training data); real-world indoor scenes for testing

numbers.eval_set_note: 4 real scenarios (Fridge far target, Door obstacle, Chair turn-around, Table sharp turn), 8 trials each; without provided instructions
numbers.extra: trained in sim, deployed zero-shot; model generates its own instructions

numbers_note: The abstract's averages (18.8% -> 56.3% task success; fixed-instruction correctness 22.5% -> 75.5%) are not in the tables I was given as such; the 56.3% average is consistent with the per-scenario values (mean of 37.5, 62.5, 62.5, 62.5). The fixed-instruction correctness results are only in figures. The baseline's mean success is 18.75%, consistent with 18.8%. Scenario-level real-world test set is small (8 trials per scenario).
results: In zero-shot sim-to-real closed-loop navigation, Action QFormer raises average task success from 18.8% to 56.3% versus the direct-fusion baseline and drives the instruction OOD rate from about 97-100% to 0.0%. With instructions given, the gap shrinks (Action QFormer 87.5-100% vs baseline 25-87.5%) but remains large in the harder scenarios. Mechanistic analyses show clearer left-right distinction in the action-facing representation and less broad upstream rewriting.
limitations: Evaluated only on small-scale real navigation (8 trials per scenario, 4 scenarios), single-frame input and one backbone; compared only against a self-built direct-fusion baseline, not against other VLA or navigation methods.
Does not solve obstacle-aware instruction planning; failures persist when the model picks an unsuitable grounding target for avoidance.

Mechanistic claims are correlational and partly qualitative (attention-focus effect is not universal; vision-frozen variant shows larger attention shifts); batch configurations differ between baseline and Action QFormer.
